1.pericope_label: The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see. Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand... I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the title recurs over six later chapters and marks off a collection of utterances on the future of the surrounding nations, then raises the question of authenticity and answers it: the objection from style rests on no sufficient evidence, and the objection that the prophecy anticipates Babylon's fall too distinctly implies a view of prophecy which excludes divinely given foreknowledge. He reads the mountain as a bare one where no trees would hide the standard, observes that the same words were used earlier of Israel's invaders and here of its avengers, takes the shaking of the hand for the gesture of generals pointing at the city to be destroyed, and notes that the term sanctified is applied even to fierce tribes as appointed for the work, just as a later chapter calls Cyrus the anointed of the Lord. Delitzsch argues from style on the other side of the same question, that one word here is peculiarly this prophet's and its combination with another so unusual that one could hardly expect it in two unrelated authors; he counts a threefold signal, the banner on a bald mountain, the voice raised high and the shaking of the hand, all favourites with this prophet, and has the summoned rejoicing with the pride of men intoxicated by victory.

Gill makes the title a prophecy concerning Babylon, noting that the Greek and Arabic render the word vision and that it signifies taking up a speech against a place. He offers a high mountain in Media or Persia for the banner, or else Babylon itself, called a mountain not for its situation, since it lay on a plain, but for its eminence; and he says the Medes and Persians are called sanctified not because sanctified by the Spirit but because set apart in God's counsel for a special work, the command reaching them by a secret instinct. Calvin explains why a collection of such oracles was needed at all: when great changes take place, some think God sports with human affairs and others that everything is driven by the blind violence of fortune, and few are aware that these things are appointed by his purpose, there being nothing of which it is harder to convince men than that providence governs the world. He reports the reading that makes the mountain a particular one but prefers it taken indefinitely, of a signal drawing a vast assembly from distant countries, and he alone stops at the oddity that a private man is here made to command the Medes and Persians.

Wesley says the title is commonly given to sad prophecies, grievous burdens to those on whom they are laid, and thinks the prophet intimates that the enemy would come out of the mountainous country of Media. Clarke assumes the authenticity that Ellicott argues for, taking this and the following chapter as one prophecy of Babylon's fall to the Medes and Persians delivered two hundred years before the event. He removes a word from the verse about the banner as useless, on the authority of an ancient manuscript and the Latin, and on the sanctified ones says nothing is plainer than that the verb means to consecrate or appoint to a purpose, adopting a bishop's rendering, my enrolled warriors.
Henry hears the other sense of burden: it is a lesson they would be loath to learn, and those who will not make the word of God their rest will find it made a burden to them.

debates.question: What does the word burden mean in the title?

positions.view: A prophecy or speech taken up against a place; the Greek and Arabic render the word vision.
A lesson men are loath to learn; those who will not make God's word their rest find it made a burden to them.
A title commonly given to sad prophecies, grievous to those on whom they are laid.

debates.question: Which mountain is the banner raised upon?

positions.view: A high mountain in Media or Persia, or else Babylon itself, eminent though it lay on a plain.
Better taken indefinitely, of a signal drawing a vast assembly from distant countries.
A bare mountain, where no trees would hide the standard.
The mountainous country of Media, out of which the enemy would come.

debates.question: In what sense are the invaders God's sanctified ones?

positions.view: Set apart in God's counsel for a special work, not sanctified by the Spirit, the command reaching them by a secret instinct.
Consecrated or appointed to a purpose, so that the phrase means enrolled warriors.
Appointed for the work although fierce tribes, as a later chapter calls Cyrus the anointed of the Lord.

outliers.note: Alone notices that a private man is here made to command the Medes and Persians, which he could not do unless God had fortified him.
Deletes a word from the verse about the banner as useless and weakening, where every other voice translates it.

themes: The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see.
Lift ye up a banner upon the high mountain, exalt the voice unto them, shake the hand, that they may go into the gates of the nobles.
I have commanded my sanctified ones, I have also called my mighty ones for mine anger, even them that rejoice in my highness.

4.pericope_label: The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people... Howl ye; for the day of the LORD is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty... and their faces shall be as flames

schools.summary: Ellicott has the prophet hear the tramp of forces mustering on the mountains north of Babylonia and grants candidly that his geography was probably vague. He reads the end of heaven as cosmology, representing an age in which the earth was an extended plain with the sky rising like a vault above it, so that the phrase stands for the furthest limit of discovery; notes that the verse about the day almost verbally reproduces a line in an earlier prophet, and that the phrase for destruction from the Almighty carries the emphasis of assonance and perhaps of etymology, since many derive the divine name from the verb to destroy. On the terror he finds the image of powerless agony in prophets earlier and later and its most striking parallel in a psalm probably contemporary with this chapter, and on the faces like flames he grants the comparison seems at first to describe those who cause terror rather than those who feel it, explaining it as the moment when ordinary pallor flashes into intensity and the eyeballs glare. Delitzsch passes over both geography and imagery, noting only how fast the command is executed, the great army already coming down from the hills.

Gill hears the noise on the mountains of Media or on those bordering Chaldea, takes the end of heaven for the east on a rabbi's authority, and notes that the old paraphrase has the ends of the earth, which suits Persia and Media since between them and Babylon lay all Assyria. He has the Babylonians called to lament instead of the feasting they were engaged in the night the city fell, and observes that though some two hundred and fifty years lay between the prophecy and the event it is represented as at hand to show its certainty. Calvin explains the manner of the whole passage, that the prophets are not satisfied with speaking unless they give a bold picture, since plain words do not strike us so powerfully as figures delineating a living resemblance. He turns the mustering into providence, the operations of war not springing up at random, for though everything disorderly is vomited out by the passions of men God rules on high and armed men are nothing but his instruments; he says the prophet does not really instruct the Babylonians as if he hoped it would profit but uses direct address for emphasis, that the day is so called because when the Lord delays judgment he seems to cease from his office like a judge who does not ascend the bench, and that the boiling cruelty of Babylonian hearts is here ridiculed indirectly.

Clarke supplies the army's composition from another prophet, who calls it an assembly of great nations from the north country and names three kingdoms with the Median kings; he cites the same rabbi as Gill for the east and reports one word of the clause missing from a manuscript and the Syriac. Wesley says the words about the end of heaven are not to be understood strictly, makes the Medes and Persians only a rod in God's hand, takes the faces for faces inflamed with rage and torment, and has the Babylonians amazed to see so impregnable a city taken so easily.
Henry calls the passage a very elegant and lively description of the confusion to come, God being about to appear in wrath.

debates.question: What is meant by the end of heaven?

positions.view: The east, on a rabbi's authority, the old paraphrase reading the ends of the earth, which suits Persia and Media.
The same rabbi's reading, with the note that one word of the clause is missing from a manuscript and the Syriac.
Ancient cosmology: the earth an extended plain under a vaulted sky, so the phrase means the furthest limit of discovery.
The words are not to be understood strictly.

debates.question: Why is a summons to howl addressed to men who have no intention of howling?

positions.view: The prophet does not really instruct them as if he hoped it would profit, but uses direct address for emphasis.
They are called to lament instead of the feasting they were engaged in the night the city fell.
The passage is an elegant and lively description of the confusion to come.

debates.question: How can the faces of terrified men be as flames?

positions.view: The comparison seems at first to fit those who cause terror, but means the moment when ordinary pallor flashes into intensity and the eyeballs glare.
Faces inflamed with rage and torment.
An indirect ridicule of the cruelty that boiled in Babylonian hearts, God enfeebling them until their courage falls at once.

outliers.note: Leaves the geography and the imagery alone and remarks only on the speed with which the command is executed.
Hears assonance in the Hebrew of destruction from the Almighty and suggests destruction from the destroyer as a fair equivalent.

themes: The noise of a multitude in the mountains, like as of a great people; a tumultuous noise of the kingdoms of nations gathered together: the Lord of hosts mustereth the host of the battle.
They come from a far country, from the end of heaven, even the Lord, and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.
Howl ye; for the day of the Lord is at hand; it shall come as a destruction from the Almighty.
Therefore shall all hands be faint, and every man’s heart shall melt:
And they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them; they shall be in pain as a woman that travaileth: they shall be amazed one at another; their faces shall be as flames.

9.pericope_label: Behold, the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger... For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light... Therefore I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the constellation, the noun meaning foolhardy or impious and rendered Orion elsewhere, and points to a widely diffused legend behind it, since the Persian name for it is Nimrod and the Arabian Giant, while in Greek myth Orion is a giant hunter slain by Zeus for outrage against the gods. He states plainly that the words in their first application had a figurative and not a literal fulfilment, such imagery being at all times the natural symbolism of a time of terror; on the precious man he hears in both Hebrew words for man the frailty of man's nature and notes that the gold of Ophir was proverbial; and on the shaking he finds the same terms used later of the great day, carried beyond the overthrow of Babylon to every world-power that resists the righteousness of God. Delitzsch hears the voice of God revealing his purpose, a visitation punishing the wicked, humbling the proud and depopulating the countries, and takes the two prefixes of the last verse as causative, explaining the therefore: because the wrath of God falls upon men, every creature which is not itself the object of the judgment becomes a medium in the infliction of it.

Gill is explicit that the darkened heavens are to be understood not literally but figuratively, expressive of a dispensation with no light, no comfort and no hope, the celestial bodies frowning and declaring the displeasure of him that dwells there; yet he reports at the end of the passage that some think the shaking was literally fulfilled at the taking of the city, with thunders and lightnings. He takes the world for the kingdom of Babylon, so called for its extent and population as the Roman empire is called the whole world, leaving open whether the evil visited is the sin or its punishment, and offers three readings of the precious man: the scarcity of men after the slaughter, the resolve of the Medes to spare none however much gold was offered, or the fear that would keep men from taking arms for pay. Calvin asks why the day should be called terrible when nothing is more desirable than to have God present, and answers that one must consider who is addressed, since the prophets describe God according to the diversity of the hearers, merciful to the merciful and severe to the ungodly. He says the prophets add extravagant modes of speaking that place God's anger before our eyes, and yet do not go beyond what took place, since no image is so alarming that the reality is not more terrible; makes Babylon a kind of world because it seemed to occupy nearly the whole earth, yet nothing so lofty that God cannot seize it with one finger; and says the pictures console the godly, who are distressed when it is well with the wicked.

Clarke supplies the poetics of the passage: Hebrew poets express prosperity and the advancement of kingdoms by images from the most striking parts of nature, the heavenly bodies shining with increased splendour and never setting, the moon like the meridian sun and the sun's light augmented sevenfold, while destruction is drawn by the opposite images, the stars obscured, the moon withdrawing her light, the earth quaking, all things tending toward their original chaos. For the world he gives classical parallels, the Greek word used of the Roman empire and of Judea and Minos calling Crete his world, and on the precious man he has the conquerors accept no ransom for either the poor man or the honourable, all falling by the sword or going captive. Wesley finds words heaped together to signify the extremity of anger, notes that constellations consist of many stars and so give greater light, makes the world the Babylonish empire, and calls the shaking a poetical and prophetical description of horrors, as if heaven and earth were about to meet together.

debates.question: Are the darkened heavens literal or figurative?

positions.view: Not literal but figurative, expressive of a dispensation with no light, comfort or hope.
Figurative in their first application; such imagery is the natural symbolism of a time of terror.
Extravagant modes of speaking which nonetheless fall short of the reality they describe.
A poetical description of horrors, as if heaven and earth were about to meet.

debates.question: What is the world that God will punish?

positions.view: The kingdom of Babylon, so called for its extent and population, as the Roman empire is called the whole world.
An empire called a world, as the Greek term was used of the Roman empire and as Minos called Crete his world.
Babylon, which seemed to occupy nearly the whole earth, yet is not so lofty that God cannot seize it with one finger.

debates.question: What does it mean that a man shall be made more precious than fine gold?

positions.view: Either the scarcity of men after the slaughter, or the Medes' refusal of bribes, or fear keeping men from taking arms for pay.
No ransom is accepted for poor man or honourable; all fall by the sword or go captive.
Both Hebrew words for man express the frailty of his nature, and few would be left.

outliers.note: Reads the last verse grammatically, taking the two prefixes as causative and inferring that every creature not itself the object of judgment becomes a medium of it.
Traces the constellation's name through Persian and Arabian legend to the Greek myth of Orion the giant hunter.

themes: Behold, the day of the Lord cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger, to lay the land desolate: and he shall destroy the sinners thereof out of it.
For the stars of heaven and the constellations thereof shall not give their light: the sun shall be darkened in his going forth, and the moon shall not cause her light to shine.
And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible.
I will make a man more precious than fine gold; even a man than the golden wedge of Ophir.
Therefore I will shake the heavens, and the earth shall remove out of her place, in the wrath of the Lord of hosts, and in the day of his fierce anger.

14.pericope_label: And it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up... Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver... Their bows also shall dash the young men to pieces

schools.summary: Delitzsch calls Babylon the market of the world in central Asia and therefore a rendezvous for the most diverse nations, a great and motley mass of foreigners now scattered in the wildest flight, and quotes a Greek tragedian's phrase for such a mixed multitude. He distinguishes those found, meaning those taken in the city by the invading conquerors, from those caught, meaning those overtaken in their flight, and insists that the bows do not stand for the bowmen but that the arrows shot from them do the dashing. Ellicott cites the same tragic line for the same purpose, adding that some would return to their own lands though without a leader; divides the two clauses of the fifteenth verse exactly as Delitzsch does; hears the sixteenth verse behind the dread beatitude the exiles pronounced on the ministers of a righteous vengeance, and observes that such outrages were then, as they have been ever since, the inevitable accompaniments of the capture of a besieged city; and makes the Medes a mixed people, Aryan conquerors mingled with an earlier race, differing in this from the Persians, who were pure Iranians in both race and creed.

Gill reports the variants of the opening clause without deciding among them, the Syriac reading they shall be and the Greek and Arabic they that are left, and adds a rabbi's view that the fugitives are people of other nations who happened to be in Babylon when it was taken. He sees the dashing of the infants as a retaliation for what Babylon had done to the Jews and takes the phrase before their eyes to govern the clauses that follow as well; and he says the naming of the Medes at last explains who the sanctified and mighty ones were, the Persians being included though only the Medes are named, since Cyrus was sent by the king of Media and served as his general, treating the naming of a nation some hundreds of years before the event as a strong proof of the truth of prophecy and of divine revelation. Calvin makes the flight military, the auxiliary and hired troops of no avail, timorous as roes and scattered as sheep, keeping neither their ranks nor any order; notes a rival rendering that refers the second clause of the fifteenth verse to old men already worn out with age but keeps his own; brings in the historian's report that by Cyrus's command they slew everyone met at the beginning of the night and next day all who had not laid down their arms; calls the treatment of the infants the utmost pitch of ferocity, the more shocking for being done before the parents; argues that the prediction could not have been human conjecture, since no jealousies existed between the two peoples and the Medes then had no power to harm Babylon; and rejects the reading that has the children used in place of arrows, conceding that we do not read the Medes exercised so great cruelty and that the city flourished long afterwards.

Clarke finds a plain defect in the opening sentence, the subject of the proposition being lost, and prefers the Greek supplement of the remnant to a manuscript's the inhabitant, which he grants makes a tolerably good sense. He presses that none escape, neither those who flee singly, dispersed and in confusion, nor those who endeavour to retreat in more regular and compact bodies, and prefers a Greek manuscript variant as properly expressive of the Hebrew; explains that no offer of gold or silver will buy a life, since rage and cruelty get the better of avarice, and cites the epic scenes in which the vanquished appeal to the pity and the greed of the victor; and reports that the Persians used bows three cubits long, so that with a metal bow of that length a soldier might dash as well as shoot. Wesley says the fugitives were soldiers of other nations whom Babylon had hired, and that the indifference to gold is to be understood comparatively, the Medes pursuing the destruction of the people more eagerly than the getting of spoil.

debates.question: Who or what is like the chased roe?

positions.view: The sentence has a plain defect and the subject is lost; the Greek supplies the remnant, a manuscript the inhabitant.
The versions differ and he does not decide; a rabbi takes the fugitives for foreigners caught in the city.
The mixed multitude of nations gathered in Babylon, scattered on the fall of the imperial city.
The hired auxiliaries, who keep neither their ranks nor any order.
The soldiers of other nations whom she had hired to assist her.

debates.question: How do the two clauses about the slain divide?

positions.view: Those taken in the city by the conquerors, and those overtaken in their flight.
Those who flee singly in confusion, and those who retreat in compact bodies; neither escapes.
A rival rendering refers the second clause to old men worn out with age, which he rejects.

debates.question: Why do the Medes despise silver and gold?

positions.view: No ransom will buy a life; their rage and cruelty overcome all motives of avarice.
The indifference is comparative: they pursue destruction more eagerly than spoil.

outliers.note: Turns ethnographer, making the Medes a mixed people of Aryan conquerors over an earlier race, unlike the pure Iranian Persians.
Concedes against his own text that we do not read the Medes exercised such cruelty, and that Babylon flourished for a long period after the calamity.

themes: And it shall be as the chased roe, and as a sheep that no man taketh up: they shall every man turn to his own people, and flee every one into his own land.
Every one that is found shall be thrust through; and every one that is joined unto them shall fall by the sword.
Their children also shall be dashed to pieces before their eyes; their houses shall be spoiled, and their wives ravished.
Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it.
Their bows also shall dash the young men to pieces; and they shall have no pity on the fruit of the womb; their eye shall not spare children.

19.pericope_label: And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah... And the wild beasts of the islands shall cry in their desolate houses... and her days shall not be prolonged

schools.summary: Ellicott says the words paint the impression the great city made upon all who saw it even in the prophet's own time, and gathers the witnesses: the king who exulted in the greatness of a city he claimed to have built though his work was mainly that of a restorer, the Greek historian who called it the most famous and strongest of the cities of Assyria and adorned beyond any city his eyes had ever looked on, and the tragedian's recurring epithet of gold-abounding Babylon. He notes that the comparison with the cities of the plain had clearly become proverbial, takes the word Arabian in its widest extent for all the nomadic tribes of the Bedouin type, and finds a literal fulfilment in their shrinking from the site, partly because it is desolate and partly from a superstitious horror. On the animals he reads the terms generically, the groaners probably horned owls and the screamers ostriches, and the shaggy ones either goats, or a grotesque mythical form like the Greek goat-god, or most probably a species of baboon; and he finds a false etymology under the received rendering of the last creature, the word strictly meaning wailers, while the phrase for desolate houses is literally among their widows, closely resembling the word for castles. Delitzsch reads the epithets historically, ornament of kingdoms because the city was the centre of many conquered kingdoms which now avenge themselves upon it, and the pride of the Chaldeans because it was the old dwelling-place of the lowlanders, related to the mountain tribes of the north-east though of another origin and different manners.

Gill notes that the word here rendered glory is the same one rendered roe earlier in the chapter, so that Babylon was once a pleasant roe and is now a chased one; he calls it the first and most ancient kingdom and the largest at the time of its fall, the head of gold of the dream image and the lady of kingdoms. He cites a traveller of the emperor Hadrian's time who said that Babylon, the greatest city the sun ever saw, had nothing left of it but a wall, and adds that what now bears the name is a new city built in another place; and on the animals he lists what the versions and the rabbis offer without deciding, monstrous and astonishing creatures, apes, martens or sables of the weasel kind, a word close to the Arabic for wild cats, and then cats, sirens, hyenas, onocentaurs and owls. Calvin explains why the prophets speak so, leaving no room for the compassion by which men relieve their minds, whereas the godly under chastisement keep the confident hope that the Lord will not altogether destroy them, from which he draws the rule that we ought not to judge from outward appearances, since we often think the children of God ruined when their salvation is at hand. He takes the verb for continuance, so that there is no hope of restoring the place, and finds the sharpest proof in the Arab, since the site must be marvellously forsaken to be disregarded by a wandering people who had left a barren country to feed flocks and hunt; he confesses that he cannot easily say how the animal names ought to be translated, given the diversity among translators, since the use of these things did not continue and the Jews have not retained the knowledge; and he faces the delay honestly, that Babylon was not so speedily overturned and that the shortness of the time is asserted because the beginnings of the ruin were soon seen.

Clarke measures rather than expounds, giving on the lowest ancient account a regular square forty-five miles in compass, inclosed by a wall two hundred feet high and fifty broad, with a hundred gates of brass, and reckoning about a hundred and twenty years from the first of Hezekiah to the first of Nebuchadnezzar, under whom the city reached its height. He calls the received word for palaces in the last verse a plain mistake, so corrected in two manuscripts and in three ancient versions, and reaches for a Homeric hymn on sea creatures stabling where men had lived, a passage of Milton that might be taken for a translation though not so designed, and the Persian couplet in which the spider holds the veil in Caesar's palace and the owl stands sentinel on the watch-tower. Wesley says only that the most noble of all the kingdoms and the beautiful seat of the Chaldean monarchy shall be totally and irrecoverably destroyed, that the Arabians dwelt in tents and wandered where they could find pasture, and that the learned agree the creatures named are frightful and solitary.

Henry finds the same wordplay as Gill without depending on him, that the word signifies a pleasant roe while the city becomes the chased roe of the earlier verse, and he allows the city its titles, the head of gold, the lady of kingdoms, the praise of the whole earth. On the comparison with the cities of the plain he grants the difference and keeps the force: the destruction was not so miraculous, nor so sudden, but as effectual, though gradual.

debates.question: What creatures are meant by the names in the last two verses?

positions.view: The versions and rabbis offer monstrous creatures, apes, martens or sables, wild cats, sirens, hyenas, onocentaurs and owls; he does not decide.
He cannot say, given the diversity among translators and the lost knowledge of these things; whether quadruped or bird is of little importance.
The terms are generic: groaners are probably horned owls, screamers ostriches, and the shaggy ones goats, a grotesque, or most probably a baboon.
The learned agree only that they are frightful and solitary creatures.

debates.question: How close is the parallel with Sodom and Gomorrah?

positions.view: The phrase had clearly become proverbial for desolation.
Not so miraculous nor so sudden, but as effectual, though gradual.

debates.question: Was the desolation as total and as swift as the oracle says?

positions.view: Total and verified: a traveller found nothing left but a wall, and what now bears the name is a new city elsewhere.
The city was not so speedily overturned; the shortness of the time is asserted because the beginnings of ruin were soon seen.

outliers.note: Leaves exposition for measurement and for poetry, giving the city's dimensions and quoting a Persian couplet on the spider in Caesar's palace.
Reads the epithets as ethnography of the lowland Chaldeans rather than as praise of the city's splendour.

themes: And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees’ excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.
It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there.
But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there.
And the wild beasts of the islands shall cry in their desolate houses, and dragons in their pleasant palaces: and her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged.
